1310.title: Communities differ
1310.hook: Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative rabbis perform same-sex weddings; Orthodox rabbis do not
1310.howItsDone: Rabbis in the Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative movements officiate at same-sex weddings; Orthodox rabbis do not, holding to their reading of Jewish law.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was yichud, and your line was the first moment: a few minutes alone, with friends at the door. Today, a question Jewish communities answer differently.

Two schools of rabbis, the house of Hillel and the house of Shammai, disagreed about marriage law. Not about flowers or music: about who was permitted to marry whom. The stakes were high. By one school's rules, some marriages the other allowed should not have happened. And yet the Mishnah records something striking. The house of Shammai did not hold back from marrying into families of the house of Hillel, and the house of Hillel did not hold back from the house of Shammai. They disagreed, and they still married each other's children.
screen: `HILLEL AND SHAMMAI DISAGREE.` → `ABOUT WHO MAY MARRY WHOM.` → `AND THEY STILL MARRIED IN.`

segments.voice: Here is today's difference, said plainly. Rabbis in the Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative movements perform weddings for same-sex couples; their movements allow it, though an individual rabbi may still decline. Orthodox rabbis do not. Orthodox rabbis hold that Torah law, as their tradition reads it, does not allow such a marriage, and they keep to that reading. The Conservative movement reached its answer through its own process of Jewish legal reasoning. Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism understand tradition as something each generation carries forward and reshapes. Each works from Torah and the rabbis, takes the question seriously, and arrives in a different place. You met these and these back in your first year. The Talmud tells of a long argument between Hillel's school and Shammai's, until a heavenly voice says both are the words of the living God, and the practical law follows Hillel. Why Hillel? Because his students were gentle and humble, and taught Shammai's view alongside their own, even putting it first. In Hebrew: elu va'elu, these and these. On an ordinary day, that looks like this. Families sometimes span more than one movement. A guest at a wedding follows that community's customs. People can hold their own view firmly and still describe another's accurately, without mockery. This lesson doesn't settle the question; it describes who says what. The old rabbis left a model: argue honestly, teach the other side fairly, and keep coming to each other's tables.
screen: `SAID PLAINLY: WHO DOES, WHO DOESN'T.` · `EACH ANSWER HAS ITS REASONS.` · `THESE AND THESE.` · `ARGUE, AND STILL SHARE A TABLE.` · then, large: `COMMUNITIES DIFFER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a community not your own, a congregation, a family, a group of friends, that does something differently from the way you would, and let a few real faces from it come. Notice any urge to win the argument and let it sit; look instead for one thing in them you can honestly respect, their care or their seriousness, and hold it for a while.
Communities differ: on same-sex weddings, and on much else, Jewish movements answer differently, each from its reading of the tradition. Today's word.
Your line: communities differ. Each side can be told so fairly the other would nod. Same time tomorrow.

1311.title: Peace in the home
1311.hook: a high value in Jewish family life
1311.howItsDone: Jewish tradition counts shalom bayit, peace in the home, as a high value in family life; teachers draw on texts like God's softened report of Sarah's words and Hillel's call to love and pursue peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was communities differ: these and these, argued honestly, each side taught fairly. Today, the smallest community there is: one home.

Sarah is inside the tent, listening. Outside, a guest tells Abraham that by this time next year, Sarah will have a son. She laughs to herself. In the King James words, she says: "After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?" A verse later, God speaks to Abraham about that laugh and repeats what she said. Except the repeat is different. Listen closely, because today's word hides in the part that goes missing.
screen: `SARAH LAUGHS IN THE TENT.` → `"MY LORD BEING OLD ALSO."` → `GOD REPEATS IT, DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: You met this page of Talmud in your first year; today, what it means for a home. When God tells Abraham what Sarah said, the King James has: "Shall I of a surety bear a child, which am old?" Sarah's age stays in. Abraham's is gone. She had said, my lord is old too; God reports only, I am old. The Talmud notices and draws a lesson: great is peace, for even the Holy One altered words for its sake. Nobody needs to carry every sharp word from one spouse to the other. Peace is also something you chase. Hillel taught: be among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace. Tradition tells of Aaron going to each side of a quarrel separately, telling each how much the other regretted it, until they met and embraced. And it's small and daily. The Talmud asks: if you can afford only one light, for Shabbat or for Hanukkah, which comes first? The Shabbat lamp in the home, for the sake of shalom bayit: a lit house, where nobody trips in the dark and tempers don't flare. Peace starts with being able to see each other. Shalom bayit is not silence, and it's not keeping up appearances. Teachers of this value say clearly that it never asks anyone to stay where they are not safe. It means a home where people are gentle on purpose, choose their words with care, and keep making the first move toward each other.
screen: `THE WORDS GOD LEFT OUT.` · `LOVING PEACE, PURSUING PEACE.` · `A LAMP SO WE CAN SEE.` · `NOT SILENCE, NOT DANGER.` · then, large: `PEACE AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you live with, or those closest to you, and one small friction between you right now: a sharp word, a chore, a silence gone on a little long. Choose one small move toward peace, a kind word or a sharp sentence you decide not to pass along, and hold it until it feels doable. And if home is ever not safe, please reach out: local emergency help, or in the US, call or text 988.
Shalom bayit: peace in the home. Pursued, not waited for, and built from small choices, like the words God left out for Sarah and Abraham. Today's word.
Your line: peace at home. Somebody has to go after it first. Rest well.

1312.title: Ending with dignity
1312.hook: a divorce document, and a hope for kindness on both sides
1312.howItsDone: In traditional Jewish law a marriage ends with a get, a divorce document written by a scribe and given by the husband to the wife before a rabbinic court and witnesses; some couples today also sign a prenuptial agreement meant to ensure a get is never withheld.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shalom bayit, and your line was peace at home. Today, the hard case: when a home can't hold its peace any longer.

A scribe dips a quill. Around the table sit a rabbinic court of three and two witnesses, and across from them, two people who once stood under a canopy together. The scribe writes a short document by hand, on purpose, for this one couple, their names spelled out with care. It is folded, then placed into her hands, and she takes it. That is all. No shouting, no verdict about who was right. Jewish law knows that some marriages end. The question it keeps asking is how.
screen: `A COURT OF THREE.` → `A DOCUMENT WRITTEN BY HAND.` → `PLACED INTO HER HANDS.`

segments.voice: The document is called a get, and its root is in the Torah. In Deuteronomy, the old Jewish Publication Society translation describes a husband who "writeth her a bill of divorcement, and giveth it in her hand." It is written. A divorce in Jewish law isn't a mood or a slammed door; it's a careful act before witnesses, so no one is left wondering whether they are free. Clarity is its own kind of kindness. It is given into a hand: the ending happens person to person. In traditional law the husband gives and the wife receives, and both must do it willingly. And the sorrow is allowed. The prophet Malachi has God say, "For I hate putting away." The Talmud adds a picture some readers never forget: when a man divorces the wife of his youth, even the altar sheds tears. Divorce is permitted, and it is still a loss worth grieving. Now the hard part, said plainly. Because the get must be given freely, a spouse can refuse to give it, and a woman can be left unable to remarry. She is called an agunah, a chained woman. Rabbis and communities have worked on this for a long time, and today some couples sign agreements before the wedding so that no one is ever trapped. Underneath it all is a hope: kindness on both sides, even at the end. A marriage that began with blessings can close with honesty, clear words, and no one humiliated.
screen: `IT IS WRITTEN.` · `GIVEN INTO A HAND.` · `EVEN THE ALTAR SHEDS TEARS.` · `NO ONE LEFT CHAINED.` · then, large: `END WITH DIGNITY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something in your life that is ending, or should: a job, a habit, a friendship that has run its course. Ask, a few breaths apart: is the ending clear, is it person to person rather than a vanishing act, and is there anything kind I could still say? Let one honest, gentle sentence form, and if you pray, hold the people on the other side of that ending in your prayer.
Ending with dignity. A get written by hand, given into a hand, a loss allowed to be a loss, and no one left chained. Today's word.
Your line: end with dignity. An ending can still be clear, and still be gentle. See you tomorrow.

1313.title: Conversion
1313.hook: study, commitment, and usually immersion in a mikveh
1313.howItsDone: A person converting to Judaism usually studies with a rabbi, appears before a rabbinic court, and immerses in a mikveh; in traditional practice men are also circumcised. The convert takes a Hebrew name, often as son or daughter of Abraham and Sarah. Movements differ on the requirements.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was end with dignity: a get given into a hand, and no one left chained. Today, a beginning instead.

A widow on a dusty road, her mother-in-law telling her to turn back. Go home, the older woman says; your own people are there. Her sister-in-law kisses her and goes. But Ruth, a Moabite with every reason to leave, holds on. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, she says: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." She walks into Bethlehem a stranger. The book that carries her name ends with a family tree, and at the end of that tree is King David. Ruth is the story Jews tell about joining.
screen: `TURN BACK, SAYS NAOMI.` → `RUTH HOLDS ON.` → `YOUR PEOPLE, MY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: You met Ruth on that road, and the heart of a stranger, in earlier years. Today, how joining actually happens. It's called giyur, conversion, from ger, which in the Torah means a stranger living among the people; later the rabbis used the same word for someone who joins. The door isn't pushed open. The Talmud describes a would-be convert being asked, honestly, why they want to join a people that has often suffered, and told about some of the commandments, easy and hard. If they say, I know, and I am still not worthy, they are accepted. The questions are a kind of respect: this is a real choice. Then come study and commitment: time spent learning, living a Jewish year, and in traditional practice, coming before a rabbinic court of three to accept the commandments. Movements differ on the details and on who may sit on that court. Usually there is immersion in a mikveh, the ritual pool, and for men, in traditional practice, circumcision, or a symbolic drop of blood if already circumcised. The person goes into the water and comes up a Jew. A convert takes a Hebrew name, often as son or daughter of Abraham and Sarah. And the past is closed: the Talmud teaches that you must not remind a convert of what they used to be. The Torah says, "And a stranger shalt thou not oppress; for ye know the heart of a stranger." A ger is not a guest. A ger is family.
screen: `THE DOOR IS NOT PUSHED OPEN.` · `STUDY, AND A COURT OF THREE.` · `INTO THE WATER.` · `A HEBREW NAME.` · then, large: `A NEW NAME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who joined something you were born into, a family by marriage, a team, a neighborhood, a country, a faith, and notice how long they've been trying to belong. On each breath out, let go of one way you still treat them as new, and let one small word of welcome form. If you pray, you can pray for someone you know who has chosen a new path.
Giyur. Conversion: honest questions, study, the court, the water, and a Hebrew name as a child of Abraham and Sarah. Today's word.
Your line: a new name. Whoever chose to come in is home. I'll be here tomorrow.

1314.title: Visiting the sick
1314.hook: the Talmud says a visitor takes away a sixtieth of the illness (Nedarim 39b)
1314.howItsDone: Visiting the sick, bikur cholim, is a commandment and an act of kindness in Jewish life; some synagogues have a bikur cholim group that organizes visits, calls, meals and errands for members who are ill or homebound.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was giyur, and your line was a new name. Today, a commandment anyone can do with a pair of shoes and an hour.

One sixtieth. That's the claim in the Talmud, tractate Nedarim: whoever visits a sick person takes away a sixtieth of the illness. The rabbis around the table do the math out loud. Then sixty visitors should cure him completely? They don't laugh it off, and they don't take it literally. They add conditions and keep going. Nobody in the conversation says the visit is pointless. The argument is only about how much it carries.
screen: `ONE SIXTIETH.` → `THEN SIXTY VISITORS?` → `THE VISIT CARRIES SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew it's bikur cholim, visiting the sick, and you met it in your first year at Abraham's tent. There Abraham is recovering from his circumcision, and the text says the Lord appeared to him. The Talmud reads that as God visiting the sick, and draws a line: as God visits the sick, so should you. Visiting is walking in God's ways. On the same page in Nedarim, a student of Rabbi Akiva falls ill and nobody comes. Akiva goes himself. The floor is swept and sprinkled for the sick man, he recovers, and the student says, Rabbi, you have brought me back to life. Akiva walks out and teaches: anyone who does not visit the sick is like one who sheds blood. Strong words, to make a point: absence costs something. Later teachers give practical advice. Don't stay so long you exhaust the person. Sit at their level, not looming over the bed. Ask what they need: the floor swept, the groceries, the dog walked. And pray while you're there, the tradition says, because you see their need with your own eyes. There's a short line people say: may God have mercy on you among all the sick of Israel. Even the prayer refuses to leave anyone alone. A sixtieth is small. It is not nothing.
screen: `GOD VISITED ABRAHAM.` · `AKIVA GOES HIMSELF.` · `SHORT VISITS, LOW CHAIRS.` · `PRAY WHERE YOU CAN SEE.` · then, large: `VISITING LIGHTENS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who is sick or stuck at home right now, and picture where they are sitting today. Ask what they might need that isn't advice, and plan a visit, small and real: a call, a doorstep drop-off, a short visit in a low chair. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
Visiting the sick. Bikur cholim: the way God visited Abraham, Akiva at a lonely student's bedside, a short visit, and a prayer at the bedside. Today's word.
Your line: visiting lightens. Showing up, even briefly, carries more than it seems. Until tomorrow.

1315.title: The last confession
1315.hook: a short prayer of confession said near death
1315.howItsDone: When a Jew is gravely ill, a family member, friend or rabbi may gently offer to say the vidui with them, a short confession found in prayer books; it is often followed by the Shema.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was visiting lightens: Akiva at the bedside of a student nobody else came to see. Today we stay at the bedside, for the hardest conversation there is.

How do you tell someone who is very sick that it might be time to make their peace, without telling them they're dying? Jewish tradition has a sentence ready, and it's a strange, kind one. Before the confession, the visitor says something like: many have confessed and not died, and many have not confessed and died. Saying this prayer is not a verdict. It doesn't summon anything. It's simply good to be ready.
screen: `THE HARDEST CONVERSATION.` → `CONFESSING IS NOT A VERDICT.` → `IT'S GOOD TO BE READY.`

segments.voice: The prayer is vidui, confession, a word you met in your second year. The same word names the confession said on Yom Kippur, when a whole congregation admits its wrongs together. This one is said alone, or with a few people close by, near the end of life. The Talmud teaches that when a person falls ill and is close to death, they are told: confess. It's not a punishment. The Mishnah teaches that whoever confesses has a share in the world to come. Confession is a door, not a sentence. And it's gentle. The codes say not to raise it in front of people who will break down crying, so the sick person isn't frightened. If they can't speak, they can confess in their heart. If they can't manage the full text, a few words are enough. The tradition bends toward the person in the bed. Wordings vary, but the short vidui acknowledges that healing and death are both in God's hands, asks for healing if it can be, asks that if death comes it be counted as atonement for wrongs done, and asks for care for the family left behind. It's honest about both outcomes at once. Traditionally, the last words are the Shema: hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one. The line from childhood bedtime becomes the last line of all. Vidui isn't about fear. It's about not leaving the important things unsaid.
screen: `THEY TELL HIM: CONFESS.` · `GENTLE, NEVER FRIGHTENING.` · `HONEST ABOUT BOTH OUTCOMES.` · `IT ENDS WITH THE SHEMA.` · then, large: `READY.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself one quiet question, nothing morbid: if today were my last, what would I wish I'd said? Let one thing come, an apology owed, a thank-you never sent, an I love you, and breathe with it; if you pray, you can say the Shema slowly, or sit in silence. If thoughts of death ever feel heavy rather than gentle, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
Vidui. Confession: said near the end of life, gently, honest about healing and death, and closing with the Shema. Today's word.
Your line: ready. Nothing important left unsaid, to anyone you love. Go gently.

1316.title: Never alone
1316.hook: after death the body is watched over until burial
1316.howItsDone: In Jewish communities that keep this custom, family members or volunteers take turns sitting with the body from death until the funeral, a practice called shemira; the shomer often reads Psalms.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was vidui, and your line was ready. This week walked from communities that differ, to peace at home, to endings, beginnings, and the bedside. Today it ends past the last breath.

Two in the morning. A quiet room at a funeral home, one lamp on. In the next room, under a sheet, lies a woman who died yesterday afternoon. In this room, in a plain chair, sits someone with a book of Psalms open on their knee. Maybe a grandson. Maybe a stranger from the synagogue who signed up for the night shift. They read a little, they sit, they keep awake. At six, someone else will take the chair. Between death and burial, she will not be left by herself for a minute.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `A CHAIR AND A BOOK OF PSALMS.` → `SHE IS NOT LEFT ALONE.`

segments.voice: Shomer means a guard, a keeper, a watcher, and you met it in your very first year, in Cain's mouth. After Abel is killed, God asks Cain where his brother is, and Cain answers, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "am I my brother's keeper?" Keeper there is shomer. Cain meant no. The one in the chair at two in the morning is answering yes. The practice is called shemira, watching. Why watch someone who has died? The body once held a person made in the image of God, and Jewish law treats it with honor: kavod ha-met, honor for the dead. It isn't set aside like an object while the paperwork gets done. Some also teach that the soul lingers near the body until burial, and the watcher keeps it company. Tradition says to read Psalms, or simply to sit in quiet, and not to eat or chat in the room. The Talmud even exempts someone watching the dead from certain other commandments, because they are busy with this one. Family watch, if they can. When they can't, volunteers from the community step in, sometimes in shifts through the night, often for someone they never met. So this week ends where it began, with communities: different practices, different homes, and in the end, a chair by the door, and someone in it.
screen: `AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?` · `HONOR FOR THE DEAD.` · `PSALMS, OR QUIET.` · `FAMILY, OR A STRANGER.` · then, large: `NEVER ALONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has died, not their last day but an ordinary one: their voice in the kitchen, a joke they told too often. Keep them company for a few breaths, the way a shomer would, and if you pray, read a psalm for them or sit in silence. If a loss ever feels too heavy to carry alone, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
Shomer. The keeper who sits with the body from death to burial, reading Psalms or keeping quiet, answering Cain's question with yes. Today's word.
Your line: never alone. Someone always takes the chair. A week done; see you tomorrow.
